name: INA225AIDGKR
title: 36 V common-mode, zero-drift, bidirectional current-shunt monitor with pin-selectable gain of 25, 50, 100 or 200 V/V
summary: INA225 amplifies the small voltage across a current shunt and gives a voltage output, with the shunt anywhere from 0 V to 36 V common mode whatever its own 2.7 V to 36 V supply. Two logic pins, GS0 and GS1, pick a gain of 25, 50, 100 or 200 V/V, and the gain may be changed while running. A REF pin sets the output level for zero current, so it measures in one direction (REF at ground) or both (REF at a mid-level voltage). Zero-drift input: ±150 µV maximum offset, 0.5 µV/°C maximum drift. INA225AIDGKR is the 8-pin VSSOP (MSOP) part on a 2500-piece reel.
key_figures: 25, 50, 100, 200 V/V, set by GS0 and GS1

circuits.title: Microcontroller-configured gain selection
circuits.description: High-side shunt between the power supply and the load. IN+ takes the supply end, IN- the load end; REF is grounded, so OUT reads current in one direction above ground. OUT drives an ADC read by a microcontroller, and two microcontroller GPIO lines drive GS0 and GS1, so firmware can step the gain to keep the output inside the ADC's linear range as the current changes. The INA225 runs from 5 V with a 0.1 µF bypass.

circuits.title: Input filter
circuits.description: A differential RC low-pass sits between the shunt and the inputs: a series resistor RS of 10 Ω or less in each lead and CF across IN+ and IN-, giving f-3dB = 1 / (2π RS CF). Every larger RS adds gain error because the input bias currents are unequal once a differential voltage is present. REF, GS0 and GS1 go to ground: one-direction sensing at 25 V/V. Supply 5 V with a 0.1 µF bypass.

circuits.title: Transient protection above 36 V
circuits.description: For common-mode transients beyond 36 V: a resistor RPROTECT of about 10 Ω in each input lead and a zener from each input pin to ground. The resistors give the zeners a working impedance; low-power zeners in SOT-523 or SOD-523 suffice for short transients. Only zeners or zener-type absorbers respond fast enough. REF, GS0 and GS1 grounded (25 V/V, one direction); 5 V supply with a 0.1 µF bypass.

circuits.title: Shutting down the device
circuits.description: The part has no shutdown pin; a logic buffer driven by a shutdown control line supplies VS, with the 0.1 µF bypass on VS. While unpowered, each input still sees about 525 kΩ to REF. REF connects through a selector to one of three sources: a reference voltage directly, an op-amp follower of a divider on that reference, or ground; the drain from the shunt depends on which source REF sees and whether it is powered. GS0, GS1 and GND go to ground.

circuits.title: Unidirectional operation
circuits.description: REF is grounded, so the output sits near ground with no sense voltage and rises with current flowing from IN+ to IN-. The shunt is on the high side between supply and load. Two changeover switches set GS0 and GS1 each to VS or ground to pick the gain. Supply 2.7 V to 36 V with a 0.1 µF bypass.

circuits.title: Bidirectional operation
circuits.description: REF is driven from a reference so the output rests at VREF with no sense voltage, going above it for current from IN+ to IN- and below it for current the other way. A selector feeds REF either straight from the reference voltage or from an op-amp follower of a divider across it. VREF may be anywhere from 0 V to VS, usually mid-supply. GS0 and GS1 each switch to VS or ground. Supply 2.7 V to 36 V with a 0.1 µF bypass.

operation.text: A zero-drift current-sense amplifier for common-mode voltages up to 36 V. Its bandwidth reaches 125 kHz at 100 V/V. Four gains, 25, 50, 100 and 200 V/V, are chosen with the GS0 and GS1 pins and may be changed during operation, which widens the range of input signal that can be measured accurately.

GS0 and GS1 are logic inputs read against VIL (0.6 V max) and VIH (2 V min). Both low gives 25 V/V, GS1 alone high 50 V/V, GS0 alone high 100 V/V, both high 200 V/V. Most designs tie them to fixed levels; driven from a controller they allow a wider dynamic range or an automatic gain control loop.

The fixed errors of the amplifier, mostly its offset, are a smaller part of a larger shunt voltage, so a bigger shunt is more accurate but dissipates more. The largest shunt follows from the full-scale current, the input range of the stage after the INA225 and the gain chosen. Example: 10 A full scale and a 4 V output at 25 V/V need 160 mV, a 16 mΩ shunt dissipating 1.6 W, with offset error about 0.1 %. At 100 V/V the same 4 V needs 40 mV, a 4 mΩ shunt at 400 mW, but offset error rises fourfold to about 0.38 %.

Filter at the inputs rather than at the output, where a filter would undo the buffered output's low source impedance. Keep each series filter resistor at 10 Ω or below. An internal bias network makes the two input bias currents differ once the inputs see a differential signal; through external series resistance this lowers the voltage reaching the pins below that across the shunt, which appears as gain error.

There is no shutdown pin. The supply current is low enough to feed VS from a logic gate or a transistor switch. Unpowered, each input has about 525 kΩ (500 kΩ feedback plus 25 kΩ input resistor) to REF. With REF grounded that is 525 kΩ from the shunt to ground; with a powered reference or op amp on REF it is 525 kΩ to that voltage; with an unpowered source on REF the current depends on that source's output impedance, near zero if it goes open.

Add a resistor in each input lead, ideally about 10 Ω, as working impedance for a zener from each input; larger resistors work at the cost of gain error. Use only zeners or zener-type absorbers: other transient absorbers react too slowly. Since only short transients are clamped, a 10 Ω resistor and the lowest-power zener available, in SOT-523 or SOD-523, take the least board area.

With REF grounded the output is low at zero input and rises with positive sense voltage; it cannot go below ground for negative input. How close to ground the output gets at zero input depends on the gain (7, 15, 30 and 60 mV typical at 25, 50, 100 and 200 V/V). About 10 mV on REF lifts the output above that limit and returns the output's saturation level to 10 mV, so small signals can be read; buffer whatever drives REF to avoid common-mode rejection error. REF may instead go to VS: the output then rests 200 mV below the supply and falls only for negative sense voltage. REF must never exceed VS.

A voltage on REF sets the output for zero sense voltage; the output rises above VREF for positive differential input (IN+ above IN-) and falls below it for negative. VREF can be anywhere from 0 V to VS, usually mid-supply for equal range each way, or offset when the currents in the two directions differ.

A controller reads the output through an ADC; when the output nears the top of the wanted range it changes GS0 and GS1 to a lower gain, the output steps down, and it climbs again with rising current. In the example response, gain steps from 200 to 25 V/V as load current rises from 0 to 10 A.

The inputs measure correctly at common-mode voltages above VS: VS can be 5 V while the monitored rail is at 36 V. The input pins withstand -0.3 V to +36 V whether or not the part is powered. A bypass capacitor, typically 0.1 µF, is needed for stability, as close to VS and GND as possible; noisy or high-impedance supplies may need more decoupling.

Connect IN+ and IN- to the shunt by a Kelvin (four-wire) connection so only the shunt's own resistance lies between them; any high-current copper in that path adds large error with such low shunt values. Put the 0.1 µF bypass as close as possible to VS and GND. The reference layout grounds REF, GS0 and GS1 (one direction, 25 V/V), with the bypass capacitor beside pins 2 and 3 and vias to the ground plane.
Built-in ESD protection is limited; store and handle with leads shorted or in conductive foam.
